source.title: Phydi: Initializing Parameterized Hypercomplex Neural Networks As Identity Functions
source.authors: Matteo Mancanelli; E. Grassucci; A. Uncini; D. Comminiello

record.file_problem: Text is the full paper; some figure text is garbled, but the main prose and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether initialization affects convergence and trainable depth in parameterized hypercomplex networks, using epochs to an accuracy or perplexity threshold rather than training classification error.
record.gate_note: Reported outcomes include CIFAR-10 epochs to 80% accuracy and WikiText2 epochs to a perplexity threshold. The paper also describes Fixup behavior but omits its scores; cited results from other work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study uses dynamical isometry and identity initialization to develop PHYDI and evaluates its performance in hypercomplex residual networks and Transformers. It does not test V3's plain-versus-residual training-error comparison, V4's initialization effects in plain networks, or V6's batch-normalization and Fixup comparisons. Faster convergence of the proposed residual-gating method does not establish those specific claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: PHYDI improves convergence speed and learning depth in hypercomplex convolutional and Transformer models. However, their assertion of faster convergence in every test overstates Table 1: PHResNet18 ties standard initialization at n=2 and takes more epochs at n=4. Better gradient propagation is their proposed explanation, not a separately reported gradient measurement.
record.recipe_differences: Tests a hypercomplex identity initialization against standard and weighted Kronecker initialization, measuring epochs to accuracy/perplexity thresholds; the claim versions largely concern classification error, depth shortcuts, and other initialization methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with depth, hyperparameter n, architecture and initialization; PreNorm exceeds PHYDI for small Transformer encoders, while PHYDI is reported to preserve convergence at high depth. PHResNet gains are not uniform across n and depth.

fits_no_version.finding: PHYDI usually reduces epochs to 80% CIFAR-10 accuracy in hypercomplex residual networks, especially at 152 layers. At batch size 64 it ties standard initialization for ResNet18 n=2 and is slower for n=4; at batch size 128 the ResNet50 n=3 improvement is small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Zero-initialized trainable residual gates can accelerate hypercomplex residual-network convergence, with benefits depending on depth, n and training settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Hypercomplex PostNorm Transformers diverge as depth increases, with the onset depending on n. PreNorm is best at 12 or 16 layers; normalization-free PHYDI reaches perplexity 200 in two epochs at 96 layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual gating and normalization configuration affect convergence and trainable depth in hypercomplex Transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4.1 qualitatively reports slow Fixup convergence for PHResNet18 and impaired final accuracy for deeper PHResNets, without scores or a documented matched normalization comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fixup may require adaptation for hypercomplex residual networks.

record.peer_reviewed: International Workshop on Machine Learning for Signal Processing (IEEE), 2023
record.problems: Reports convergence proxies (epochs to 80% accuracy or perplexity ≥ 200), not training classification error. Transformer numerical outcomes are mainly figure-only. Fixup comparison scores are omitted, and the paper does not state exact run counts in the provided text.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported result omitted from the extracted tables/figure description. Fixup outcomes are described qualitatively in Section 4.1 but have no reported scores and are not separate rows.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and size, stopping or regularization conditions.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation in plain convolutional networks versus identity-shortcut counterparts; very deep plain tanh networks; the specified normalization-free residual-network result.
Activation-matched initialization and signal propagation in plain networks; orthogonal-versus-Gaussian tanh comparisons; orthogonal convolution kernels and 10,000-layer plain networks.
Initial stability limits, loss recovery, curvature changes, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence below the threshold.
Batch normalization versus no batch normalization for speed and learning-rate tolerance; Fixup matching normalized residual networks in speed and stability.

record.verdict_notes: The table values are transcribed correctly. PHYDI adds zero-initialized trainable residual multipliers; WKP adds trainable weights initialized to one. These comparisons change parameterization as well as initial function. None provides a verdict on the six versions as written. Fixup's qualitative outcome is already declared in rows_left_out, so it is not a missing result.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure training classification error, CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, model size thresholds, or early stopping and regularization effects.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student problem or spurious-minimum frequency experiment.

Tests hypercomplex residual networks and hypercomplex transformers; does not compare plain versus shortcut convolutional networks. Fixup is mentioned without reported scores. Does not report training classification error.
Compares PHYDI and weighted non-identity initialization and varies hyperparameter n, but does not test the listed activation-matched, orthogonal, Gaussian, or 10,000-layer initializations.

Does not test batch normalization against no normalization in the specified real-valued MNIST, VGG/CIFAR-10, or Inception/ImageNet settings. Transformer comparisons vary normalization position, but do not measure speed of accuracy gain or learning-rate tolerance.

rows.subject: PHTransformer PostNorm
rows.operation_detail: Train with PostNorm and measure epochs to perplexity threshold.
rows.uncertainty: vertical standard error bars over multiple runs
rows.note: Text states PostNorm diverges with just 48 layers for n=2; numerical epoch values are figure-only.
rows.check: PostNorm Transformer divergence does not measure V3's convolutional comparison or V4's plain networks. The caption's perplexity ≥200 conflicts with the prose's target of 200; record epochs to reach 200. Split convergent depths from divergence at 48 layers for n=2.

rows.subject: PHTransformer PreNorm
rows.operation_detail: Train with PreNorm and measure epochs to perplexity threshold.
rows.baseline: PostNorm and PHYDI comparisons at matched settings
rows.uncertainty: vertical standard error bars over multiple runs
rows.note: Text says PreNorm performs better than PostNorm and best for small encoders with 12 or 16 layers, exceeding PHYDI; overall values are figure-only.
rows.check: PreNorm uses layer normalization, not batch normalization. This pooled row mixes depths and n values; separate the shallow-encoder advantage from deeper settings. Record epochs to reach perplexity 200 rather than ≥200.

rows.subject: PHTransformer PHYDI
rows.operation_detail: Train with PHYDI and measure epochs to perplexity threshold.
rows.baseline: PostNorm and PreNorm comparisons at matched settings
rows.uncertainty: vertical standard error bars over multiple runs
rows.note: The paper states PHYDI improves convergence and robustness in very deep models; for n=2, 3, and 4, detailed plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: PHYDI changes residual gating and removes layer normalization; it does not isolate a listed version. The two-epoch result is stated for 96 layers, not every depth from 12 to 96; its applicability to each n is not explicitly specified. Record epochs to reach perplexity 200.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: PHYDI usually lowers epochs to 80% accuracy versus standard initialization, but is equal for PHResNet18 at n=2 and slower at n=4 (R3, R21); the measurement is not training error.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: PHTransformers on WikiText2, encoder depths 12 to 96
reader_labels.reason: PostNorm diverges at some depths while PHYDI reaches the threshold at 96 layers; PreNorm is better for shallow encoders and is described as more stable as depth increases (R46-R48).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The effects vary with n and depth: PHYDI ties standard at PHResNet18 n=2, is slower at PHResNet18 n=4, and is faster in the reported deeper cases (R3, R6, R9, R21).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: PHTransformers on WikiText2, encoder depths 12 to 96
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports different convergence behavior across depth, n, and normalization configuration; PreNorm exceeds PHYDI at 12 or 16 layers, while PHYDI works at 96 layers (R46-R48).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Normalization-position comparisons show PreNorm outperforming PostNorm and PHYDI on small encoders, but this does not test batch normalization, accuracy gain, or learning-rate tolerance (R46-R48).
